name: VITA shade guide

lead: The VITA shade guide is a set of tooth-coloured tabs labelled A1 to D4 that puts a number on how light or dark teeth are. People use it to record a starting shade and see how far whitening has moved it.

A clinician holds tabs next to the tooth and picks the closest match by value (lightness) and chroma (colour intensity); instruments can also measure colour. Dental studies have examined its limits, including colour coverage gaps and differences between visual and instrument readings. In appearance communities, shade numbers serve as shorthand for how white teeth are.

paras: A dentist or the user compares tabs to the teeth in consistent lighting before whitening, then again afterwards to see the change. It is combined with whitening treatments, and photos are often taken alongside the shade.
The guide itself carries no risk because it is a measurement reference, not a treatment. Visual matching accuracy varies with lighting and the person doing the match.

chain: Tabs A1 to D4 rate tooth color
angle.text: Dentists and whitening-focused users use the VITA scale to put a number on how light teeth are before and after treatment. Tabs from A1 to D4 are matched to the tooth, so progress can be tracked. It is a measurement reference rather than a treatment and is widely used in cosmetic dentistry.

lead: The VITA classical shade guide is a set of tooth-coloured tabs, labelled A1 to D4, that dentists hold beside a patient's teeth to describe and match tooth colour. It is arranged by value (lightness) and chroma (colour intensity), with letter groups A (red-brown), B (red-yellow), C (grey) and D (red-grey) [1]. For anyone whitening their teeth to look better, it serves as a common yardstick for saying how light teeth are before and after treatment, so a change can be described as a number of shades gained [1][2].

In looksmaxxing and cosmetic dentistry, shade numbers are shorthand for how white teeth are, and results are quoted in shade steps. Wikipedia reports in-office bleaching commonly gives about 2 to 7 shades and at-home strips or trays about 1 or 2 [1].

Dental research has examined the guide itself, including its colour coverage, the accuracy of visual matching compared with instruments, and how it compares with instruments and newer guides [3][4][5][6][7]. Many whitening trials use it as the outcome scale [2][8][9][10].

paras: The classical guide groups tabs by hue letter and a number for chroma. Practitioners in whitening and prosthodontics choose the tab that looks closest to a tooth under standard lighting and record its code [1]. Dental technicians receive the selected shade when they make crowns, veneers or bridges, and a Japanese review of prosthodontic teamwork notes that shade selection with the guide is often subjective and can lead to miscommunication between dentist and laboratory [11].

Digital tools, including photography, intraoral scanners and spectrophotometers, supplement or replace visual choice. A 2024 study compared shade matching by an intraoral scanner, a spectrophotometer and visual assessment [5], and another measured the in-vivo repeatability of three intra-oral spectrophotometers [6].

Researchers frequently use the guide to measure bleaching results, for example by enrolling volunteers with teeth at shade A3 or darker and counting shade steps gained [2]. Newer trials commonly report both the classical guide and the VITA Bleachedguide, in shade guide units, alongside an instrument reading [9][10].

Wikipedia lists the expected shade gains of different products: in-office 2 to 7 shades, strips and trays 1 to 2, toothpastes 1 to 2 with continued use. It also reports that nearly half of an in-office change can rebound within a week and that re-treatment may be needed every six months to a year [1].

A 1991 study examined the colour coverage of two shade guides, and a 1998 study compared a sphere spectrophotometer with human evaluation of tooth shade [3][4]. A 2025 paper titled "How many tooth colors are there?" examines the range of natural tooth colour against fixed guides [7]. ClinicalTrials.gov lists small studies comparing visual, photographic and spectrophotometric matching, with 9 to 20 participants in the smaller ones and 210 patients in a 2026 study of how the order of shade presentation affects patient choice [12][13][14].
A 2014 randomised comparison examined selecting VITA classical shades using the VITA 3D-Master guide [15].

Studies have evaluated the guide as a measurement tool. A 1991 study examined coverage errors of two shade guides, and a 1998 study compared a sphere spectrophotometer with human evaluation of tooth shade [3][4]. ClinicalTrials.gov lists small trials comparing visual, photographic and spectrophotometric shade matching [12][13]. Clinical bleaching trials use the guide as an outcome scale [2][8].

Examples include a 40-person trial of in-office light-activated systems in volunteers with shade A3 or darker [2], a 2005 comparison of over-the-counter, in-office and at-home bleaching to reach six grades of whitening [8], and an 80-person randomised trial comparing combined in-office plus at-home bleaching with at-home bleaching alone, which found slightly higher colour change in the first week for the combined group, no significant difference at the end, and more sensitivity with the combined approach [9]. A 40-person split-mouth trial of 40% hydrogen peroxide found no significant colour difference between gel mixed at the session and gel mixed a week earlier [10]. A 50-person trial examined violet LED with 35% carbamide peroxide [16].

Shade numbers circulate in whitening advertisements, dentists' before-and-after galleries and online discussions of cosmetic dentistry. Regulation of the whitening products themselves differs by region: Wikipedia reports EU rules limiting retail hydrogen peroxide to 0.1% and the US FDA endorsing gels under 6% hydrogen peroxide or up to 16% carbamide peroxide [1].
